Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da).
